name: Pub/sub
summary: Publish one message; every subscriber gets its own copy.
howItWorks: A publisher sends a message to a topic without knowing who’s listening. The broker delivers a copy to every current subscriber. Adding a consumer means adding a subscription, with no change to the publisher. Plain pub/sub keeps no history, so an offline subscriber misses messages unless its subscription is backed by a durable queue.
analogy: A group chat. You post once and everyone in the group sees it, but people who join later don’t see what was said before.
useWhen: Fan-out: one event triggers several independent reactions
Decoupling teams, since publishers don’t need to know about consumers
Device messaging over MQTT, where each device subscribes to its own topics
avoidWhen: Work that one worker must do exactly once; that’s a queue
Consumers that need to replay history; that’s a stream
example: When an order is placed, one `OrderPlaced` message fans out to email, analytics and inventory. A year later the fraud team subscribes too, and the order service doesn’t change at all.

source: # Email, analytics and inventory each subscribe to the topic,
# usually through their own SQS queue so nothing is lost.

diagram.caption: Each message is copied to all three subscribers. While inventory is offline its copies are lost, which is why durable designs put a queue behind each subscriber.

story: Publish/subscribe grew up in the mid-1980s, on trading floors and in research labs. Trading rooms needed stock quotes and news on many screens the moment they changed. Vivek Ranadivé’s Teknekron Software Systems, founded in 1985, built an “Information Bus” that delivered that information as it became available, and its successor, TIBCO, carried the idea into enterprises. At Cornell, Ken Birman’s Isis toolkit, released in 1987, included a topic-based “news” service written by Frank Schmuck, which Birman calls “the first widely used publish-subscribe solution.”

In 1999 Andy Stanford-Clark of IBM and Arlen Nipper wrote MQTT to monitor oil pipelines over expensive satellite links, taking pub/sub to small devices on poor networks. Cloud providers later offered topics as a service: Amazon SNS in 2010, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub in 2015, built on infrastructure Google’s own products use for over 500 million messages per second.
The lines have since blurred. Durable subscriptions turn a topic into a set of queues, logs such as Kafka add replay, and MQTT, an OASIS standard since 2014, is widely used for device telemetry.

choices.why: A sender doesn’t know who is listening, so new consumers can be added years later without changing the publisher.

choices.choice: Many topics mapped onto few channels
choices.why: One group per topic created huge numbers of groups, so Isis mapped topics onto a few groups and filtered at the receiver, an approach Birman notes is still common in pub/sub products.

choices.choice: Deliver to whoever is subscribed now
choices.why: Classic pub/sub keeps nothing, which keeps latency low. Systems that can’t lose messages put a durable queue behind each subscription.
MQTT’s control messages can be as small as two bytes, because its first users paid for satellite bandwidth from remote pipelines.

OASIS publishes MQTT 3.1.1 as a standard
Google Cloud Pub/Sub becomes generally available
